doc.title: Charles Davis interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, August 23, 1997

title: Views on jazz, cool jazz and audiences
summary: Jazz deserves respect; cool jazz lost the audience; playing changes with the venue.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Do you consider jazz to be, some people call it America’s classical music, or black classical music. Do you have a sense of how jazz is — your own personal sense of how jazz should be viewed?

It should be viewed with great respect. Myself personally, you know that’s my personal opinion. Because there’s nothing like it. I mean speaking of jazz, if you’re speaking about Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker and Thelonious Monk, there’s nothing like it. It’s such a heck of a creative venue that nothing’s been created since then to equal it. It’s output, musically and emotionally and spiritually.
Why do you think jazz, when it moved into the bebop era, that it lost a good portion of its audience?
Well it wasn’t bebop that lost the audience. When they turned to the cool jazz is when it lost its audience I think.
It lost its sizzle. I think when it got too cool, the guys just became very cold as far as what they were doing. They were more into themselves then in dealing with the reality of their audience.
Well that’s a good statement. Musicians relating to their audience.
Yeah. Well that’s what it’s about.
Do you feel that your playing changes from one venue to the next?

Yes, it does, according to what you’re dealing with. I think it’s according to the way you are sometimes, what you’ll play. What motivates one audience doesn’t motivate the next audience so you have to keep that in mind.
